issues.legal_issue: An ancient family estate may be impartible by custom independently of a later family agreement or legislation.
material_facts: The estate had a long history as a zamindari and was treated as impartible before the 1889 family settlement.
The settlement described the estate as already impartible and recorded the family’s recognition of that character.
The estate was included in the schedule to legislation concerning impartible estates.
issues.conclusion: The estate was an ancient impartible estate by custom and was not made impartible for the first time by the 1889 agreement or by the legislation of 1902 or 1904.
issues.legal_principle: Impartibility may arise from ancient custom. The court relied on Gopala Krishna v. Sarvagna Krishna, Nargunt Lutchmedavanah v. Vengama Naidoo, Raja Ras Venkata Mahipathy Ramkrishna v. Court of Wards, and Pushavathi Viziaram Gajapathi Rai Maina v. Pushavathi Visweswar. The terms of the family agreement and the estate’s inclusion in the schedule to the Madras Impartible Estates Act, 1904, supported the finding that the agreement and legislation recognized, rather than first created, impartibility.

predicates.impartible_estate_case: The proceeding concerns whether a family estate is impartible.
predicates.estate_has_long_impartible_history: The estate had a longstanding history of being held as impartible.
predicates.family_agreement_recognizes_existing_imp: The family agreement described the estate as already impartible rather than creating that status for the first time.

issues.definition: When an impartible-estate proceeding concerns an estate with a longstanding history of impartibility and the family agreement recognizes that existing status, the estate is impartible by custom.

issues.legal_issue: Properties incorporated into an ancient impartible estate retain their impartible character when they do not vest in the government, and junior family members acquire no right by birth to partition them.
material_facts: The properties claimed for partition were outside the territorial limits of the estate and did not vest in the government under the abolition legislation.
The properties had been incorporated into the impartible estate.
The estate was impartible by ancient custom.
The claimants sought partition as junior members of the family.
issues.conclusion: The properties retained their impartible character, and the junior members had no right to partition them.
issues.legal_principle: The abolition legislation repealed the Madras Impartible Estates Act, 1904, in its application to the estate transferred to the government, but did not affect properties outside that transferred estate; the 1904 Act continued to apply to those properties. Incorporated property acquired the impartible character of the estate, which could not be lost without statutory intervention. Custom may outlive the conditions that gave rise to it; the maxim cessante ratione legis cessat ipsa lex did not apply. Junior members of an ancient impartible joint-family estate acquire no right in the property by birth and therefore have no right to partition. The court relied on sections 3(b) and 66 of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, section 4 of the Madras Impartible Estates Act, 1904, Rai Kishore Singh v. Mst. Gahanabai, C.I.T. Punjab v. Dewan Krishna Kishore, Raja Velugoti v. Raja Rajeshwara Rao, Pushavathi Viziaram Gajapathi Rai Maina v. Pushavathi Visweswar, and Anant Bhikappa v. Shankar Ramchandra.

rule.if: partition_claim_over_family_property and property_was_incorporated_into_impartible_estate and property_did_not_vest_in_government and estate_is_impartible_by_custom

predicates.partition_claim_over_family_property: Junior members of a family sought partition of family property.
predicates.property_was_incorporated_into_impartibl: The property had been incorporated into an impartible estate.
predicates.property_did_not_vest_in_government: The property was not transferred to the government under the abolition measure.
predicates.estate_is_impartible_by_custom: The estate had been found to be impartible by custom.

issues.definition: When junior members seek partition of property incorporated into an estate that is impartible by custom, and the property did not vest in the government, they have no right to partition it.

issues.legal_issue: A pre-existing contractual maintenance obligation continues against estate property retained by the holder after abolition, even when compensation is payable for property transferred to the government.
material_facts: A family agreement required maintenance payments from the income of the estate and its properties.
The abolition legislation transferred part of the estate to the government, but other properties remained with the holder.
The claimants had received or were entitled to compensation-related payments under the abolition legislation.
The statutory provisions addressed apportionment of compensation but did not expressly extinguish the maintenance obligation against retained properties.
issues.conclusion: The maintenance obligation under the agreement continued after abolition, and the claimants could recover any shortfall after crediting income attributable to compensation.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 45(1), 45(2), 45(4), and 45(5) of the Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, govern apportionment of compensation among maintenance-holders; they do not, absent express language, extinguish contractual maintenance rights against property not transferred to the government. Sections 9 and 14(2) of the Madras Impartible Estates Act, 1904, also concern maintenance rights and existing arrangements. The court held that the legislature should not be taken to have released retained property from its obligation to contribute to maintenance without express words.

predicates.post_abolition_maintenance_claim: A claimant sought maintenance after an estate was abolished or transferred under a statutory scheme.
predicates.maintenance_obligation_arose_under_famil: A family agreement required maintenance to be paid from estate income.
predicates.some_estate_property_remained_with_holde: Some estate property remained with the holder rather than being transferred to the government.
predicates.compensation_provisions_addressed_transf: The statutory compensation provisions dealt with property transferred to the government and did not expressly extinguish obligations against retained property.

issues.definition: When a post-abolition maintenance claim rests on a family agreement, some estate property remains with the holder, and compensation provisions address transferred property without extinguishing obligations against retained property, contractual maintenance continues against that retained property.

issues.legal_issue: Descendants whose maintenance claim under a family agreement has already been rejected cannot obtain maintenance by reasserting the claim under another clause of the agreement.
material_facts: Two claimants were illegitimate sons of a family member whose branch was addressed in the agreement, and another claimant was the son of one of them.
A prior proceeding had rejected the illegitimate sons’ claim to maintenance under the agreement and Hindu law.
The claimants later relied alternatively on a clause concerning the nearest relatives of a deceased maintenance-holder.
The court found that the agreement used the relevant kinship term in a context that did not include the claimants.
issues.conclusion: The claimants were not entitled to maintenance under the agreement; the earlier decision barred the reasserted claim, and the alternative interpretation of the agreement was also rejected.
issues.legal_principle: A prior adjudication of the same entitlement binds the claimants under res judicata, and a successor claimant cannot claim greater rights than the person through whom the claim is made. The agreement’s reference to descendants and to nearest relatives had to be read in context; the latter provision did not extend the allowance to the claimants. The court relied on the prior Judicial Committee decision concerning the same maintenance claim.

rule.if: maintenance_claim_by_descendants and ((same_entitlement_was_previously_adjudicated and claimants_are_illegitimate_descendants) or (claim_relies_on_kinship_clause and agreement_uses_kinship_term_narrowly))

predicates.maintenance_claim_by_descendants: Descendants sought maintenance under a family agreement.
predicates.same_entitlement_was_previously_adjudica: A prior proceeding had adjudicated the same entitlement to maintenance.
predicates.claimants_are_illegitimate_descendants: The claimants were illegitimate descendants of the family member through whom they claimed.
predicates.claim_relies_on_kinship_clause: The claimants relied on a clause granting an allowance to certain relatives of a deceased recipient.
predicates.agreement_uses_kinship_term_narrowly: The agreement’s wording and context limited the relevant kinship term so that it did not include the claimants.

issues.definition: When descendants seek maintenance under an agreement and the same entitlement was previously adjudicated for illegitimate descendants, or the agreement’s kinship clause does not include them, maintenance is unavailable to them.

issues.legal_issue: A family member cannot obtain a further division of an object when the evidence shows that the object was already divided.
material_facts: The claimants sought a share of a golden howdah as part of their partition claim.
The will and related evidence showed that the golden and silver articles had been dealt with in an earlier division.
The evidence showed that the golden howdah had already been divided and that nothing remained for further division.
issues.conclusion: The claimants were not entitled to a further division of the golden howdah.
issues.legal_principle: The court construed the will and the evidence of the earlier division as showing that the golden howdah had already been divided; it therefore affirmed the rejection of a further division claim.

predicates.partition_claim_for_family_object: A claimant sought division of an object as part of a family partition claim.
predicates.evidence_shows_object_was_already_divide: The evidence showed that the object had already been divided and that no part remained for a further division.

issues.definition: When a claimant seeks division of a family object and the evidence shows that it was already divided, no further division of the object is available.
